name: Spiritism
info: Spiritism, or Kardecist spiritism, is a reincarnationist and spiritualist doctrine founded in France in 1857 by Allan Kardec, which holds that spirits communicate through mediums and return to life in order to improve, and which is strongest today in Brazil.

facts.origin: France, in the mid-19th century, with the publication of The Spirits’ Book in 1857 by Hippolyte Léon Denizard Rivail, writing as Allan Kardec, after he observed table-turning and the spiritualist currents of Europe and the United States.
facts.founder: Allan Kardec (Hippolyte Léon Denizard Rivail), a French writer and educator, who coined the term spiritisme in 1857 and directed the Revue Spirite until his death in 1869.
facts.scriptures: The Spiritist Codification, five basic works by Kardec published between 1857 and 1868: The Spirits’ Book, The Mediums’ Book, The Gospel According to Spiritism, Heaven and Hell, and The Genesis, with complementary works such as What is Spiritism?, the Spiritist Review and Posthumous Works.
facts.followers: About 13 million worldwide according to data from 2005, in 36 countries according to the International Spiritist Council; about 3.8 million in Brazil in the census of 2010, the country with the most followers.

t: Spiritists believe in one God, in the immortality of the spirit, in reincarnation as the means of moral and material improvement, and in useful communication with spirits through mediums.
The doctrine rests on five works by Allan Kardec, the Spiritist Codification of 1857–1868, and has no priestly hierarchy: its basic unit is the Spiritist centre, a non-profit association.
Brazil has the most Spiritists, about 3.8 million in the census of 2010, and there the doctrine was banned by the penal code of 1890 until the code of 1940 ended the prohibition.
dyk: Kardec’s own account of table-turning is that, to obtain longer answers, he had the table knock a number of times for each letter of the alphabet; asked what it was, the being that answered declared itself a spirit.
ev: The events at the home of the Fox sisters in Hydesville begin on 31 March; many Spiritists mark the date as the first milestone of modern mediumistic manifestations
Kardec publishes The Spirits’ Book on 18 April and coins the term spiritisme
Spiritism reaches Brazil in the 1860s; the Brazilian Spiritist Federation dates its arrival to this year
Kardec dies; Spiritism is said to have gained 7 million followers since 1857
The Brazilian Spiritist Federation is founded in Rio de Janeiro on 2 January
Brazil’s penal code bans the practice of Spiritism, punishing it with up to six months in prison
Brazil’s penal code of 1940 ends the official prohibition of Spiritism
The International Spiritist Council is constituted in Madrid on 28 November

sections.origins:
Kardecist spiritism, also called Kardecism or simply Spiritism (Espiritismo in Portuguese and Spanish, spiritisme in French), is a reincarnationist and spiritualist doctrine established in France in the mid-19th century by the writer and educator Hippolyte Léon Denizard Rivail, who wrote as Allan Kardec. He coined the term spiritisme in 1857 and defined it as “the doctrine founded on the existence, manifestations, and teachings of spirits”. It emerged as a new religious movement in tandem with spiritualism, and ideas and practices of communication with spirits had spread through North America and Europe since the 1850s.

Spiritists believe that mediumistic phenomena are universal and have always existed, and they cite biblical cases such as Saul’s consultation of the Witch of Endor. In the 19th century attention to mediumship grew in the United States and Europe, in the form of strange noises, knocks on furniture and objects that moved without apparent cause, as in table-turning. Many Spiritists mark 31 March 1848, the beginning of the events at the home of the Fox sisters in Hydesville, as the first milestone of modern mediumistic manifestations.

Kardec observed table-turning and, to obtain longer answers, had the table knock a number of times for each letter of the alphabet. The being that answered declared, when questioned about its nature, that it was a spirit. He questioned whether muscular action could explain such movements, but Michael Faraday’s experiments, published in 1853, showed that table-turning was caused by the ideomotor effect. Victor Hugo, in exile on Jersey from 1851 to 1855, took part in many sessions and came to believe he had contacted his late daughter Léopoldine and writers such as Shakespeare and Dante.
sections.beliefs:
Spiritism was founded, in the doctrine’s own dating, on 18 April 1857, with the publication of The Spirits’ Book, which presents dialogues with disembodied spirits who speak through mediums from the standpoint of Christian morality. Its basic principles include the existence and unity of God, whom Spiritists regard as the supreme intelligence and primary cause of all things, and the immortality of the spirit, which acts on matter through a “semimaterial” link called the perispirit. Spirits return to matter as many times as needed in order to improve; Spiritists reject metempsychosis. All spirits are held to be created equal, “simple and ignorant”, with free will and a destiny of perfection, and a law of cause and effect governs their fate. Spiritism also teaches a plurality of inhabited worlds.

Jesus, held to be created by God, is the guide and model of humanity, and Spiritists do not ascribe a divine nature to him. They reject the Trinity and salvation by grace, and they summarise Christian morality as “Outside of charity, there is no salvation”, charity meaning benevolence towards all, indulgence towards the imperfections of others and forgiveness of offences.

The doctrine has no priestly hierarchy and no institutionalised rituals such as baptism or a marriage ceremony. It excludes exorcism, sacramental formulas, horoscopes, amulets, incense, vestments, altars and offerings to images, and all its practice is free of charge. It has no official symbol; the vine branch engraved in The Spirits’ Book is taken as an image of the relation between spirit and body.
sections.texts:
The Spiritist Codification consists of five basic works published between 1857 and 1868. The Spirits’ Book (1857) contains the doctrine’s fundamental principles. The Mediums’ Book (1861) treats the investigative side of Spiritism and the phenomena its followers attribute to spirits. The Gospel According to Spiritism (1864) reads the canonical gospels from the Spiritist standpoint, with attention to worship, prayer and charity. Heaven and Hell (1865) examines the fear of death, heaven, the Christian hell, purgatory and eternal punishment, and includes dialogues that purportedly took place between Kardec and various spirits. The Genesis (1868) takes up the creation of the universe, the nature of the spirit and of so-called miracles.

Kardec’s complementary works include What is Spiritism? (1859), an introductory work, and the periodical Revue Spirite, which he founded in January 1858 and directed until he died in 1869; the International Spiritist Council now publishes it quarterly. In January 1890 the directors of the Parisian Society of Spiritist Studies released his unpublished writings as Posthumous Works. Sic Cogito (1892) by B. P. Hașdeu is a work on Spiritism as a philosophy.

Kardec described Spiritism as at once a science of observation and a philosophical doctrine, and also, in other writings, as religious. Spiritists do not agree on whether it is a religion. At the International Spiritist Congress in Paris in 1925 a proposal to remove its religious aspect was opposed by Léon Denis, who called it not the “religion of the future” but the “future of religions”.
sections.spread:
From 1857 to 1869, the year of Kardec’s death, Spiritism gained 7 million followers, by one count. It reached Mexico in the decades of 1850 to 1860, where it attracted the intellectual elite with its proposals of modernism, anticlerical reform and free thought; Refugio Indalecio González published El Evangelio Según el Espiritismo in Spanish there in 1872. In Spain the Marquis of Flórida read a bill for its official teaching on 26 August 1873, and in Romania B. P. Hașdeu, after the death of his daughter Iulia, practised it at Câmpina and wrote Sic Cogito in 1892.

It arrived in Brazil in the 1860s; the Brazilian Spiritist Federation dates it to 1865. Through Bezerra de Menezes and Chico Xavier it became popular across much of the country. Brazil has the most followers, and Cuba, where Spiritism has been present since the 19th century, had 400 Spiritist centres in 2011 with 200 more being registered.

Spiritism is also associated with other currents: it influenced Santería, Umbanda and New Age movements. The term “Kardecist spiritism” arose partly to distinguish Kardec’s doctrine from Afro-Brazilian religions such as Umbanda, which had begun to call themselves Spiritist. The Pan-American Spiritist Confederation, founded in Argentina on 5 October 1946, brings together Spiritists mainly from Latin America.
sections.community:
The basic unit of organisation is the Spiritist centre, also called a Spiritist society or house. In law it is an ordinary non-profit association, run by a president or directors elected for a term, and its members fund the centre and its charitable activities. Centres differ from Spiritualist churches in not being organised as ecclesiastical bodies, and many offer “spiritist complementary therapies”. Spiritists are strongly associated with charity, maintaining asylums, orphanages, schools and daycares; the Brazilian Spiritist Federation, founded in Rio de Janeiro on 2 January 1884, gathers about ten thousand institutions.

The International Spiritist Council, constituted in Madrid on 28 November 1992, unites national movements and has 35 associated countries; it holds the World Spiritist Congress every three years. The Pan-American Spiritist Confederation defends a secular view of Spiritism and takes positions other Spiritists contest, such as separating the doctrine from Christianity.

In Brazil the penal code of 1890 banned the practice of Spiritism and punished it with up to six months in prison; it ceased to be officially prohibited only with the code of 1940. Dissenting currents include Roustainguism, which accepts Jean-Baptiste Roustaing’s The Four Gospels and holds that Jesus had a fluidic body; Christian rationalism, which began in Santos in 1910; Ramatism; Conscientiology, systematised in 1987; and Christian Renewal, since 2002.
sections.legacy:
About 13 million Spiritists are reported worldwide for 2005, and the International Spiritist Council counts 36 member countries. In Brazil the 2010 census recorded about 3.8 million, up from 2.3 million in 2000, making Spiritists the third-largest religious group there, with the highest income and education levels of the census’s groups. Kardec is the most read French author in Brazil, with more than 25 million copies of his books sold, and Spiritist books lead bestseller lists. Brazilian television and film have drawn on Spiritist works, among them the soap opera A Viagem and the film Chico Xavier.

Spiritists also maintain a movement of health care, including the International Spiritist Medical Association, Spiritist hospitals and the physician Adolfo Bezerra de Menezes’s book on mental disorders, Insanity from a New Perspective.

Its standing is disputed. Spiritists regard their doctrine as Christian; the sociologist Antônio Flávio Pierucci says it is not a Christian religion, and many scholars call it neo-Christianity. The Catechism of the Catholic Church says Spiritism often implies divination or magical practices. The scientific consensus considers parapsychology a pseudoscience, while Alexander Moreira de Almeida calls Kardec’s approach scientific. The Theosophical Society saw Spiritist explanations as too simple, and René Guénon criticised its concept of reincarnation in The Spiritist Fallacy.

summary: Spiritism is a reincarnationist doctrine founded in France in 1857 by Allan Kardec, who held that spirits communicate through mediums and return to life to improve. Its five basic works are the Spiritist Codification of 1857 to 1868, and it has no priesthood. Brazil has the most followers, about 3.8 million in 2010.
references: John Warne Monroe, Laboratories of Faith: Mesmerism, Spiritism, and Occultism in Modern France (Cornell University Press, 2008)
Lynn L. Sharp, Secular Spirituality : Reincarnation and Spiritism in Nineteenth-Century France (Lexington Books, 2006)
notes: Source is the article ‘Kardecist spiritism’ (the saved file is titled so). Start 1857: the article says it was ‘founded on 18 April 1857’ with The Spirits’ Book; no hedge, so circa is false.

Event 1848 predates the start; it is the article’s ‘initial milestone’ as many Spiritists mark it. Event 1865: article says Brazil’s arrival was in the 1860s, FEB dates it to 1865 and the Anuário Espírita gives an earlier history. I use 1865 as the FEB’s date and say so.

Brazil follower figures: the lede says about 3.3 million (IBGE) and over 30 million sympathizers (FEB); the body says 3.8 million from the 2010 census. The profile uses 3.8 million and leaves out 3.3 million and 30 million. Worldwide: lede ‘over 13 million’; Demographics ‘about 13 million, data from 2005’. ICS: 36 countries (lede, Demographics) versus 35 associated countries (Organizations); both are given, attributed.

Left out: the Beatitudes section, the list of scientists named as investigators of mediumship, the Brazilian professions’ associations, the soap-opera list, the ideomotor/Faraday detail beyond one sentence. The article’s ‘7 million followers’ 1857–1869 is quoted as the article’s own figure.

Article contradicts itself or is unclear: ‘Sic Congito’ in the Romania section is a typo for Sic Cogito (1892); the article’s heading ‘Spiriticism’ likewise. The article says both that Spiritism ‘has no official symbol’ and discusses the vine branch; kept as stated. The article says Kardec ‘clearly asserts’ Spiritism is a religion; I give only that Spiritists disagree.

Faith map: Cuba starts 1900 because the article says only ‘since the 19th century’, 2011 for the 400 centres; Argentina 1946 (CEPA founding); Mexico 1860 (‘decades of 1850–1860’); Brazil level 1 although the third-largest group, because the article gives no region-wide majority. Coordinates are general geography.
